newsitem.title: UK: Europe will lag in car electronics - report.
newsitem.headline: Europe will lag in car electronics - report.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
A coming electronics revolution in the auto industry is set to boost U.S., Japanese and South Korean manufacturers at the expense of the Europeans, according to a report published Wednesday.
Over the next 10 years, computer power will gradually take more of the risk out of driving, and may also be able to protect the ultimate innocents in traffic accidents: pedestrians.
Radar sensors will enable drivers to latch on to the car in front and maintain a steady, safe distance between the vehicles, the report from the Economist Intelligence Unit said.
"Within five years, people will be driving cars in which electronic systems will take over many decisions and actions," the report said.
Computers will increasingly take over management of engines, brakes and steering.
"The use of electronic airbags will not only extend to protect car occupants from side impacts, but will also protect pedestrians struck by cars," the report said.
According to the report, the use of electronics could increase power by up 50 percent and improve fuel consumption by 25 percent while cutting harmful emissions by between 40 percent and 90 percent.

The value of the world automotive electronics market will be $84 billion by 2005, more than double 1995's $37 billion. This is the equivalent to an average content per car of more than $1,700, compared with $920 now, the report said.

The North American Free Trade Agreement nations of the United States, Canada and Mexico will lead this market, accounting for $26.5 billion worth of business by 2005, compared with $13.0 billion last year and an expected $20.6 billion in 2000.

As consumers clamour for the latest computerized gimmicks, car companies with in-house expertise will be in the fast lane. "Car makers who have electronics subsidiaries or electronics affiliates are at a distinct advantage," the report said.

"Ford, General Motors, the Japanese and South Korean manufacturers are better placed than the Europeans. In particular, Daewoo, Hyundai and Samsung Co., which starts building cars in 1998, will benefit from being part of a large group which includes a dominant electronics company," the report said.

Koreans will win a competitive edge by building cars around electronics systems, offering more features at lower costs. "As a result, the Koreans will be at least level with volume European manufacturers in features, electronics systems and vehicle dynamics by 2000," the report said.
